notes.h: Biotic factors: grazing and mowing in the grassland
notes.b: Biotic factors are the effects that living organisms have on each other. In a grassland they include food supply, predation, grazing, competition, parasites and disease, pollination and decomposition, and human activities such as grazing livestock, mowing and fertilising. Grazing and mowing show how one biotic factor shapes which plants can live in a habitat.
points: Grazing by rabbits, cattle or sheep and mowing keep grass short. This lets low rosette plants (plants whose leaves lie flat close to the ground) such as daisy, dandelion and plantain get light, and stops shrubs and trees from invading.
If grazing or mowing stops, taller grasses shade out the rosette plants because they grow above them and take the light. In time scrub (a tangle of woody shrubs, e.g. brambles, hawthorn) invades.
notes.tip: Grazing is herbivory: a rabbit eating grass is a primary consumer, not a predator. Keep the word predation for animals that kill and eat other animals.

notes.h: Biotic factors: decomposers, detritivores and pollinators
notes.b: Other living things work in the grassland soil and on its flowers. Some recycle dead material back into the ground, and others carry pollen between flowers.
points: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) and detritivores (animals that eat dead organic matter, e.g. earthworms, woodlice, and slugs in part) break down dead plants, dung and dead animals, returning minerals to the soil so that plants can take them up again.
Decomposition recycles carbon and nitrogen, and there is more on this in The carbon cycle, The nitrogen cycle and Bacteria and fungi.
Earthworms also drag leaves underground, mix and aerate the soil (let air into it), and improve drainage.

Pollinators such as bumblebees, hoverflies and butterflies feed on the nectar and pollen of clover, dandelion and buttercup flowers, and carry pollen between them, which is how these plants are pollinated.

notes.h: Finding feeding relationships from primary data
notes.b: To work out who eats whom in a grassland, you gather primary data, meaning information you collect yourself in the field. You then check it against what other people have already recorded.
points: Direct observation of animals feeding shows a feeding relationship at the moment it happens.
Feeding signs are evidence left behind: nibbled grass, holes in leaves, and broken snail shells at a thrush’s stone.
Droppings and pellets show what an animal ate, e.g. undigested fur and bones in the pellets of birds of prey.
The habitat where each animal was caught is a clue, e.g. aphids found on the stems they feed on.
Your findings are then checked against secondary sources (information collected by others), such as field guides, for what each species eats.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain feeding relationships using primary data from your chosen ecosystem. Name the kind of evidence (observation, feeding signs, pellets, where the animal was caught) and what it shows.

notes.h: Producers and consumers in the grassland
notes.b: Every feeding relationship starts with a green plant that makes food. Animals then feed on the plants, and on each other, in layers called trophic levels (feeding levels).
points: Producers in the grassland are grasses, clover, daisy, dandelion, buttercup and other green plants, which make food by photosynthesis.

Primary consumers (herbivores, which eat plants) in the grassland: rabbits and hares graze grass and clover; slugs and snails eat leaves; grasshoppers and caterpillars chew leaves; aphids suck sap from stems; bumblebees take nectar and pollen.

Secondary and higher consumers (carnivores, which eat animals, and omnivores, which eat both): ladybirds eat aphids; spiders catch flies, grasshoppers and other insects; ground beetles eat slugs and other invertebrates.
Song thrushes eat snails (smashing their shells on a stone) and earthworms; blackbirds eat earthworms and insects; hedgehogs eat slugs, beetles and earthworms.
Badgers eat mainly earthworms; foxes eat rabbits, mice and birds; kestrels eat wood mice, pygmy shrews and large insects.
Pygmy shrews eat small invertebrates such as beetles, spiders and woodlice.

notes.h: Grassland food chains and the food web
notes.b: A food chain follows one line of feeding, with arrows pointing from the food to the feeder. Because most animals eat more than one thing, the chains join up into a food web.
points: Worked example of grassland food chains: grass → rabbit → fox; clover leaves → slug → song thrush; plant sap → aphid → ladybird → (insect-eating bird); grass seeds and invertebrates → wood mouse → kestrel.
These chains connect into a food web. For example, the fox eats rabbits, wood mice and birds, so it is on several chains.
The earthworm feeds on dead leaves and is eaten by thrushes, blackbirds, badgers and hedgehogs, so it links the dead material in the soil to several animals above it.
Diagram: a grassland food web of 8–12 of the species listed above, with arrows pointing from the food to the feeder.
notes.tip: When you build or interpret a web from survey data, draw every arrow from the food to the feeder, and give an animal an arrow for each food it eats.

notes.h: Interdependence in the food web
notes.b: A food web shows that organisms depend on each other, so a change in one population spreads through the whole community.
points: The web shows interdependence: a change in one population affects others.
For example, if disease kills many rabbits, foxes eat more wood mice and birds, so those populations fall, and the grass grows taller because fewer rabbits graze it, shading out daisies.

An omnivore or a predator with several prey is less affected than one with a single food source, because it can switch to another food when one becomes scarce. There is more on predicting changes from webs in Energy and nutrient transfer.
notes.tip: Explain a change step by step along the web: who loses food, who gains, and what happens to the plants at the bottom.

notes.h: Predation and predator adaptations
notes.b: Predation is the best-known feeding relationship between animals. Predators have features that help them find, catch and kill their prey.
points: Predation is a feeding relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey.
Grassland examples of predation: fox (predator) and rabbit (prey); kestrel and wood mouse; ladybird and aphid; song thrush and snail.
The fox has acute hearing and smell to find prey, forward-facing eyes for judging distance, speed and sharp teeth, and hunts mostly at night, when rabbits feed.
The kestrel hovers into the wind while scanning the ground with very keen eyesight, then drops onto its prey, gripping it with sharp talons and tearing it with a hooked beak.
Spiders build webs to trap flying insects.
notes.tip: Exams ask for adaptations of a named predator, so choose one (fox or kestrel) and link each feature to its job, e.g. forward-facing eyes to judge distance. Predation means killing and eating an animal, so grazing does not count.

notes.h: Prey adaptations
notes.b: Prey animals need to spot danger early, escape, or avoid being noticed or eaten in the first place.
points: Rabbits have eyes on the sides of the head, giving an almost all-round field of view, and large mobile ears, so they can detect a predator coming from any direction.
Rabbits feed in groups so that some can watch for danger, thump the ground with a hind foot and flash the white underside of the tail as a warning, run in zigzags, and shelter in burrows.
Snails withdraw into their shells for protection.
Ladybirds have bright warning colours and a bad taste, so predators learn to avoid them.
Many caterpillars and grasshoppers are green, camouflaged against the grass, so predators find them hard to see.
notes.tip: Exams ask for adaptations of a named prey animal. Use the rabbit: give several features and say how each helps it avoid being caught.

notes.h: The predator–prey population cycle
notes.b: Predator and prey numbers rise and fall together in a repeating cycle, because each population depends on the other.
points: 1. When prey are plentiful, more predators survive and breed, so predator numbers rise.
2. More predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall.
3. With less food, predators starve or breed less, so predator numbers fall.
4. With fewer predators, prey numbers recover, and the cycle repeats.
Predator numbers peak after prey numbers, because predators need time to breed once food is plentiful. There are usually fewer predators than prey.
The classic data are the fur-trading records of the snowshoe hare and the lynx in Canada, which rose and fell in cycles of about ten years.
Diagram: a graph of predator and prey numbers against time: two out-of-step waves, the predator curve lower and peaking after the prey curve.
notes.tip: In the cycle, the predator peak comes after the prey peak, not before it or at the same time. Write the four steps in order, with the reason for each.

notes.h: How predation controls population size
notes.b: Predators do more than eat prey. They also help to set how many prey a habitat holds.
points: Predators usually take the old, sick, young or weak prey, which are the easiest to catch.

The effect of predation increases as prey become more numerous, because prey are easier to find. This helps keep the prey population near the habitat’s carrying capacity (the largest population the habitat can support). There is more on this in Carrying capacity and limiting factors.
Removing a predator can let its prey increase until it overgrazes its food.

notes.h: Competition: kinds and types (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Organisms compete when they need the same resource and there is not enough for all. Competition can be sorted by who is competing and by how the resource is shared out.
points: Competition is the struggle between organisms for a resource that is in short supply. Plants compete for light, water, minerals and space; animals compete for food, water, space or territory, shelter and mates.
If the resource is plentiful, there is no competition.

Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species. It is the most intense kind, because they have exactly the same needs, e.g. daisy rosettes crowding each other for space and light, or male blackbirds or robins defending territories that contain food and nest sites.
Interspecific competition is between different species that need the same resource, e.g. grasses and daisies competing for light, or rabbits and sheep grazing the same grass.
Contest competition: there is an active physical contest for the resource and the winner takes it, e.g. birds fighting over territory, or stags fighting over mates.

Scramble competition: each competitor gets as much as it can of a shared resource, so when it is scarce all get too little, e.g. seedlings crowded together all grow weak and thin, or aphids crowded on a stem.
notes.tip: Intra means within one species and inter means between different species, and students often swap them. Be ready to define both and give an example of each, and to separate contest from scramble.

notes.h: Effects of competition (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Competition has a cost for the organisms that lose, and this affects the whole population. Organisms also have features that help them win.
points: Competition reduces the growth, survival and breeding of the losers, and so limits population size. Its effect grows as the population becomes more crowded.

Between species, one may exclude the other from the habitat, or each may survive by using the resources in a slightly different way (different niches, meaning different roles or ways of living in the habitat). There is more on this in The niche.

Adaptations that help organisms compete: fast growth, and tall stems or climbing (e.g. ivy, brambles) in plants competing for light; deep roots for water; rapid breeding; aggressive defence of territory in animals.

notes.h: Competition in the grassland and in Ireland (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Two examples show interspecific competition at work: one in the grassland and one in Irish woodland.
points: In short, grazed or mown grass, daisies and other rosette plants get enough light. Where grass is left long, it outgrows and shades them, and they disappear (interspecific competition for light).
Irish example: grey squirrels, introduced to Ireland at Castle Forbes, Co. Longford, in 1911, compete with the native red squirrel for food, especially seeds and nuts.

Grey squirrels are larger, can digest acorns (which red squirrels digest poorly), eat hazelnuts before they ripen, and carry squirrelpox virus, which kills red squirrels but rarely harms grey squirrels. Red squirrels have disappeared from much of the area greys occupy.
Where pine marten numbers have recovered in Ireland, grey squirrels have declined and red squirrels have returned.
notes.tip: For an Irish example of competition, name the grey and red squirrel, the place and date of introduction, and give at least two reasons the grey squirrel wins.

notes.h: Symbiosis and its three types (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Some organisms do not just compete or eat each other but live together. This close partnership is called symbiosis, and it is sorted into three types by who benefits.
points: Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship in which two organisms of different species live together.
There are three types, named by who benefits: mutualism (both benefit, +/+), commensalism (one benefits and the other is unaffected, +/0) and parasitism (one benefits and the other is harmed, +/−).

Pollinators and flowers benefit each other (food for the insect, pollination for the plant), so the relationship is mutualistic, but the two don’t live together, so many biologists don’t call it symbiosis.
notes.tip: Symbiosis is the umbrella term covering all three types. It is not another word for mutualism.

notes.h: Mutualism: Rhizobium in clover roots (Higher Level only)
notes.b: In mutualism both partners gain. The first example is a bacterium that gives clover a supply of nitrogen, which is why clover can enrich grassland.
points: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) live in root nodules (small swellings) of clover and other legumes. The bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium, which the plant uses to make amino acids and proteins.
The plant gives the bacteria carbohydrates (from photosynthesis) and a protected home.
Active nodules are pink inside, from a pigment (leghaemoglobin) that controls oxygen levels for the bacteria.
This is why clover grows well in soils poor in nitrogen and enriches grassland. There is more on this in The nitrogen cycle.
To observe: dig up a clover plant, wash the roots and examine the nodules with a hand lens; cut one to see the pink colour.
notes.tip: Rhizobium in clover is the standard example of mutualism: state what each partner gives and gets. It is not commensalism or parasitism.

notes.h: Mutualism: gut microorganisms, mycorrhizae and lichens (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Mutualism is common wherever one partner can do something the other cannot. Here are three more examples, and in each the partners swap food or shelter for something they lack.
points: Cellulose-digesting microorganisms (bacteria, protists and fungi) live in the rumen (first stomach) of cattle and sheep, and in the caecum (a pouch of the gut) of rabbits. They digest the cellulose of grass, which the animal has no enzyme to digest.

The microorganisms get a warm, food-rich home, and the animal gets the products (fatty acids) as food. Rabbits also eat some of their own soft droppings to absorb nutrients released by these microorganisms.

Mycorrhizal fungi grow around and into the roots of most grassland plants and trees. The fungal hyphae (thread-like filaments) spread far through the soil, absorbing water and minerals (especially phosphate) and passing them to the plant; the plant supplies the fungus with sugars.

Lichens (e.g. on walls, rocks and tree bark around the grassland) are a fungus and an alga (or cyanobacterium) living together. The alga photosynthesises and supplies sugars; the fungus gives shelter, holds water and absorbs minerals.
Bacteria in the human gut are another example of mutualism. There is more on this in The microbiome.
notes.tip: Lichens are mutualism, not commensalism or parasitism, because both the fungus and the alga benefit.

notes.h: Commensalism (Higher Level only)
notes.b: In commensalism one partner gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed. It is easy to confuse with mutualism, so check whether the second partner really gets nothing.
points: Commensalism: one partner benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.
Mosses and lichens growing on the bark of trees get a place in the light without harming the tree.
Many bacteria living on human skin feed on dead skin cells and sweat without harming the host. There is more on this in The microbiome.

Seeds with hooks (e.g. burdock) are carried in an animal’s fur, and robins follow a gardener or grazing cattle to catch the invertebrates they disturb; both are commensal relationships, since the animal or gardener is unaffected.
notes.tip: Exams now expect commensalism with an example. Say clearly who benefits and that the other partner is unaffected (+/0).

notes.h: Parasitism and parasites in the grassland (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A parasite lives on or in another organism, the host, and feeds on it. Unlike a predator, it usually keeps its host alive.
points: Parasitism: the parasite lives in or on the host and feeds on it, harming it. A parasite usually weakens its host without killing it quickly, since it depends on the host.

Grassland ectoparasites (parasites living on the outside of the host): fleas on rabbits and hedgehogs; ticks on sheep, deer and humans. Ticks are also vectors of Lyme disease, meaning they carry it from host to host.
The rabbit flea carries the myxoma virus that causes myxomatosis, which has killed very large numbers of rabbits.

Grassland endoparasites (parasites living inside the host): liver fluke in sheep and cattle on wet pasture; roundworms and tapeworms in the gut of grazing animals. There is more on liver fluke and tapeworms in Pathogens.
Plant parasites: rust fungi on grasses and cereals.

Yellow rattle, a meadow plant, is a partial parasite: it photosynthesises but taps the roots of grasses for water and minerals, weakening the grasses so that other wild flowers can grow. For this reason it is sown when restoring wildflower meadows.
Ivy is not a parasite: it climbs trees but makes its own food and takes nothing from them.

notes.h: Effects of parasites on populations (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Parasites and disease do not usually kill many hosts quickly, but they still affect how many hosts there are.
points: Parasites and disease weaken hosts, making them easier prey and less able to breed.
Parasites spread fastest when hosts are crowded, so their effect increases with population density, like predation.

notes.h: Summary of relationships (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The signs show the effect on each partner: + for benefits, − for harmed, and 0 for unaffected. Use them to compare the five relationships.
points: Predation (+/−): a predator kills and eats its prey, e.g. fox and rabbit.
Competition (−/−): both organisms lose some of a scarce resource, e.g. grass and daisy for light, or grey and red squirrel.
Mutualism (+/+): both benefit, e.g. nitrogen-fixing bacteria in clover root nodules.
Commensalism (+/0): one benefits and the other is unaffected, e.g. mosses on tree bark.
Parasitism (+/−): the host is harmed but usually not killed quickly, e.g. a flea on a rabbit.
Predation and parasitism are both +/−. The difference is that a predator kills its prey at once and eats it, while a parasite lives on a living host over a long time.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define predation, competition, symbiosis, mutualism and parasitism and give examples. To separate predation from parasitism, say whether the victim is killed and eaten at once.

keyTerms.definition: An effect that living organisms have on each other, such as predation, competition, grazing or disease.
An organism, such as a green plant, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
An herbivore that feeds directly on producers.
An animal that kills and eats other animals, its prey.
An animal that is killed and eaten by a predator.
A bacterium or fungus that breaks down dead organic matter and returns minerals to the soil.
An animal that eats dead organic matter, such as earthworms and woodlice.
The struggle between organisms for a resource that is in short supply.
Competition between members of the same species, which have exactly the same needs.
Competition between members of different species that need the same resource.
Competition in which there is an active physical contest for a resource and the winner takes it.
Competition in which each competitor gets as much as it can of a shared resource, so that all get too little when it is scarce.
A close, long-term relationship in which two organisms of different species live together.
A symbiotic relationship in which both organisms benefit (+/+).
A symbiotic relationship in which one organism benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (+/0).
A symbiotic relationship in which the parasite lives in or on a host and feeds on it, harming it (+/−).
An organism that lives in or on a host and feeds on it, usually weakening it without killing it quickly.
The organism that a parasite lives in or on and feeds on.
A mutualistic association between a fungus and plant roots, in which the fungus supplies water and phosphate and the plant supplies sugars.
A mutualistic association of a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium, living together.

questions.prompt: What is meant by predation? Give one adaptation of a named predator and one of its named prey from an ecosystem you studied.
questions.model: Predation is a feeding relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey. Fox (predator): acute hearing and smell to find prey, forward-facing eyes for judging distance, and hunting mostly at night, when rabbits feed. Rabbit (prey): eyes on the sides of the head, giving an almost all-round field of view, so that it can see danger coming.

questions.prompt: Explain the term symbiosis, and distinguish between mutualism, commensalism and parasitism using an example of each.
questions.model: Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship in which two organisms of different species live together. Mutualism: both organisms benefit (+/+). Example: nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in root nodules of clover; they supply ammonium to the plant and the plant gives them carbohydrates. Commensalism: one organism benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (+/0). Example: mosses and lichens growing on tree bark get a place in the light without harming the tree. Parasitism: the parasite benefits and the host is harmed (+/−). Example: fleas on a rabbit feed on it and harm it, usually without killing it quickly.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between intraspecific and interspecific competition, and between contest and scramble competition. Explain how competition affects populations, using an Irish example.
questions.model: Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species, which have exactly the same needs, e.g. daisy rosettes crowding each other for space and light. Interspecific competition is between different species that need the same resource, e.g. grasses and daisies competing for light. Contest competition is an active physical contest for a resource, and the winner takes it, e.g. birds fighting over territory. Scramble competition is when each competitor gets as much as it can of a shared resource, so that when the resource is scarce all get too little, e.g. seedlings crowded together. Competition only happens when the resource is in short supply. It reduces the growth, survival and breeding of the losers, so it limits population size, and its effect grows as the population becomes more crowded. Irish example: grey squirrels, introduced to Ireland at Castle Forbes, Co. Longford, in 1911, compete with red squirrels for food such as seeds and nuts; greys can digest acorns and eat hazelnuts before they ripen, and carry squirrelpox virus, which kills red squirrels, so red squirrels have disappeared from much of the area greys occupy.
